I'd compare on rate, deal size, cycle length and cost per closed dollar rather than lead volume. And I'd raise both teams' best objections myself — that outbound leads were often warmed by marketing first, checkable via first-touch channel, and that inbound would decay without brand spend, which is probably true and unmeasurable on this data.

question: What's sales velocity useful for?
answer: Less as a number than as a decomposition. It's opportunities times deal size times win rate, divided by cycle days, so when someone says 'we need more pipeline' it turns a vague demand into a choice between four measurable levers — and more opportunities is usually the slowest and most expensive of the four. The one people undervalue is cycle length, because it compounds: halving the cycle doubles revenue per day, and a lot of cycle time turns out to be process rather than selling, like approval days and unscoped pilots, which are cheap to fix. Deal size via multi-product attach is often the next cheapest. The critical caveat is never to compute it blended across segments — dividing strategic's deal size by self-serve's cycle length produces a number that describes no business that exists.

question: A VP wants a rep leaderboard on the pipeline health dashboard. What do you say?
answer: I'd build it, on a different dashboard. The moment a diagnostic dashboard becomes an evaluative one, reps start managing the dashboard instead of the pipeline — deals get parked in early stages, close dates get pushed in bulk, and the stage data that every other chart depends on degrades. So I'd keep pipeline health diagnostic and put ranking on a coaching dashboard with the fairness controls that ranking requires: filter or flag ramping reps, normalise by segment since quotas and deal sizes differ by a factor of ten, and use trailing twelve months rather than a quarter so one large deal doesn't decide the order. I'd explain the reasoning rather than just refusing, because the VP's underlying question — who needs help — is completely legitimate and better served by a dashboard designed for it.

question: What is net revenue retention and why does it matter more than new business?
answer: NRR is what happened to the revenue from customers you already had: opening ARR plus expansion minus contraction minus churn, divided by opening, over the cohort present at the start of the period. New business is excluded deliberately — include it and you are measuring sales, not retention. It matters more in a usage business because most growth arrives without a salesperson: an account consuming more than it committed to expands with no opportunity, no session and no lead. And it compounds, which new business does not.

question: NRR is 112%. What else do you need to know?
answer: Gross retention, and the split by segment. NRR of 112 with gross of 108 is a healthy base; NRR of 112 with gross of 94 is a bucket losing six points a period, refilled by a handful of expanding accounts, and one of those churning flips the picture. The two have identical headlines and completely different futures, which is why I put gross beside NRR permanently. Then segment, because a blended figure lets one bleeding segment hide behind another's growth for quarters.

question: How do you predict churn when there is no cancellation event?
answer: Usage trend. In a business selling seats and prepaid pools, churn is a four-month fade — no cancellation record, no closed-lost, no alert — so contract status finds out at the renewal date. I flag accounts whose trailing utilisation is under the business's threshold AND falling, because level alone produces a list full of accounts that bought too much once and are not leaving. Then I join ARR to it, because eleven accounts is a number and $2.1M of ARR is a decision, and it is also what makes the list sortable in the order that matters.

question: Why never average a utilisation percentage?
answer: It weights an account with one committed seat the same as one with three and a half thousand. The correct figure is sum of used divided by sum of committed. It is the average-of-ratios trap, and in this data the two numbers differ enough to change what you would do. I also never roll utilisation across products with different units — messages and seats do not add.

question: Is overage revenue good news?
answer: It is revenue and a risk at the same time, and I report it next to the renewal date for that reason. Sustained overage is unbudgeted spend on the customer's side, so it surfaces in their procurement review, and the usual outcome is a renegotiated unit price at renewal. Celebrating it in isolation sets up a surprise two quarters later.

question: How would you measure AI deflection honestly?
answer: Net of reopens. A deflected case that came back was not deflected, it was delayed, and it cost the customer an extra round trip. I report gross and net side by side so nobody suspects the gap is being hidden. Reporting gross alone is the flattering version, and it is the version that gets an AI investment renewed on a false premise and then blamed when support load does not fall.

question: Support says a practice-org outage caused a churn. How would you check?
answer: Both tables carry AccountId, so it is provable rather than anecdotal. Take accounts with the churn-risk link on their cases and look at their ARR movements in the following months in the snapshot — contraction or churn appearing after the incident. I would also check the other direction, the accounts hit by outages that did not contract, because a claim that only looks at confirming cases is not evidence.

question: You have sixteen dashboards. How do you build the executive board?
answer: By deciding what comes off. Roughly 130 widgets exist and nine things survive, and the work is not picking the nine — most people pick a similar nine — it is defending the refusals to the people who built them. My test per number is whether a twenty percent move would change a decision this quarter, and every chart on the board has to explain one of the tiles above it. Anything that needs a paragraph to interpret will be misread in a glance, so it belongs on its own dashboard with a link.

question: How do you handle a CSAT score with a 44% response rate?
answer: Publish the response rate beside it, permanently. The average is not wrong, it just answers a narrower question than its label claims — it describes people who chose to respond, and response skews to the delighted and the furious. A satisfaction score without a response rate is an advertisement; with one it is a measurement with stated limits, and stating the limit is what makes the rest of the dashboard credible.
